q: In the course's peripheral model, which slot does EXTI fill for GPIO?
choices: Events: a separate block, not part of GPIO
Control: it is GPIO's mode register
Data in: it latches the IDR register on every pin edge
Clock gate: it powers the GPIO ports
why: GPIO itself does not interrupt. Edges are turned into interrupt requests by a separate block, EXTI.

q: Which GPIO register is the 'data in' slot?
why: IDR reads the pin levels and is read-only. ODR, BSRR and BRR are data out, and PUPDR is control.

q: What is 0xEB in binary?
why: One hex digit is exactly 4 bits: E = 1110, B = 1011. Read them in order, left digit first.

q: GPIOA->MODER resets to 0xEBFFFFFF. What are bits 27:26 (PA13's field)?
why: The second hex digit, B = 1011, covers bits 27:24. Bits 27:26 are its top two, 10: alternate function, the SWD line.

q: Which C expression clears the bits that are 1 in mask and leaves the rest of x alone?
why: AND with the inverted mask zeroes exactly the mask's bits. x | mask sets them instead, and x & mask keeps only them.

q: x = 0xFF. What is x & ~0x0C (8-bit)?
why: ~0x0C = 1111 0011 = 0xF3, and 0xFF & 0xF3 = 0xF3. Only bits 3:2 were cleared.

q: What is the offset of BSRR in a GPIO port?
why: Offsets: IDR 0x10, ODR 0x14, BSRR 0x18, LCKR 0x1C, AFR 0x20/0x24, BRR 0x28.

q: What is the offset of PUPDR in a GPIO port?
why: MODER 0x00, OTYPER 0x04, OSPEEDR 0x08, PUPDR 0x0C. Every port uses the same offsets.

q: What do the four MODER codes mean?
why: MODER: 00 input, 01 output, 10 alternate function, 11 analog. Analog is also the reset state of most pins.

q: In PUPDR, what does the code 10 mean?
why: PUPDR codes: 00 none, 01 pull-up, 10 pull-down, 11 reserved.

q: What does OTYPER bit n = 1 select for pin n?
why: OTYPER is one bit per pin: 0 push-pull (the reset value), 1 open-drain.

q: What does LCKR do?
choices: Freezes a pin's configuration until reset
Locks the output level of a pin
Blocks every interrupt coming from that port's pins
why: LCKR freezes the configuration registers of the chosen pins until the next reset. The lessons don't use it.

q: Which bits of GPIOB->MODER belong to PB3, and what value makes it an output?
why: MODER has 2 bits per pin at 2n+1:2n, so n = 3 gives bits 7:6. Output is 01; 10 would be alternate function.

q: Which PUPDR bits belong to PA12?
why: PUPDR is 2 bits per pin: 2 × 12 + 1 : 2 × 12 = 25:24.

q: PA9 needs alternate function 1. Which register and bits hold its AF number?
why: AFR[9 / 8] = AFR[1]; 9 mod 8 = 1, so bits 4·1+3 : 4·1 = 7:4. Write 0001 there.

q: Which register and bits hold pin 14's alternate-function number?
why: 14 / 8 = 1, so AFR[1]; 14 mod 8 = 6, so bits 27:24. AFR[0] bits 27:24 belong to pin 6.

q: Which BSRR bit drives pin 7 low?
why: In BSRR, bit n sets and bit n + 16 resets: 7 + 16 = 23.

q: Which GPIOA pins do not wake in analog mode, and why?
choices: PA13 and PA14: they are the SWD debug lines
PA0 and PA1: they are wired to the two user buttons
PA2 and PA3: they carry USART2
PA5 only: it drives the user LED
why: Every pin resets to 11 (analog) except PA13 and PA14, which reset to 10 (alternate function) so a debugger can reach the chip.

q: An active-low button's pin is never set to input mode. What does the program see?
choices: 'Pressed' forever: an analog pin reads 0 in IDR
Random presses: the analog pin floats and drifts between levels
'Released' forever: the pull-up holds it at 1
Correct readings: input is the reset mode
why: Pins wake analog, and an analog pin reads 0 in IDR whatever the voltage. Active low means 0 = pressed. Input mode must be written, never assumed.

q: PUPDR resets to 0x24000000. What pull does PA14 have?
why: 0x2 = 0010 is bits 31:28, so PA14 (bits 29:28) is 10, pull-down. The 4 = 0100 gives PA13 (bits 27:26) = 01, pull-up.

q: OSPEEDR resets to 0x0C000000. What does that mean?
choices: PA13 is very high speed; every other pin very low
PA2 and PA3 are very high speed
Every pin is very high speed except PA13
PA14 and PA15 are very low speed
why: 0x0C000000 has only bits 27:26 = 11, PA13's field: the debug clock line. All other fields are 00, very low.

q: What can an open-drain output do?
choices: Drive low, or let go so a pull-up makes the high
Drive high and low, like push-pull
Drive high only, with a pull-down for the low
Only read the pin, never drive it
why: Open-drain uses only the N-MOS: it pulls low or lets go. The high has to come from a resistor.

q: Two outputs share one wire; one drives high and the other low. When is that a short?
choices: When either has a pull-up enabled
why: Two push-pull outputs fighting connect 3.3 V to ground through two transistors. Open-drain outputs can share a wire; at worst both pull low.

q: Several open-drain outputs share one wire with a pull-up. What logic does the wire compute?
choices: Wired-AND: it is 1 only if every output lets go
Wired-OR: the wire is 1 if any one output drives it high
why: Any output pulling low makes the wire 0, so it is 1 only when all let go. This is how I²C puts many chips on two wires.

q: What does OSPEEDR control?
choices: The slope of each output edge
How often software can toggle the pin
The input sampling rate of IDR
why: Speed is how sharply the output switches, not the toggle rate. Faster edges radiate more noise, so choose the slowest that works.

q: A button connects a pin to GND when pressed. What does the pin need, and what does it read when pressed?
choices: A pull-up; it reads 0 when pressed
A pull-down; it reads 1 when pressed
A pull-up; it reads 1 when pressed
No resistor; it reads 0 when pressed
why: Released, the pull-up makes the pin 1; pressed, the switch pulls it to 0. That is active low.

q: An input pin with no pull resistor is connected to a released button. What does IDR show?
choices: A random level: the pin floats
The last level that was written to ODR for that pin
why: A pin connected to nothing drifts and reads randomly. That is the 'phantom presses' symptom of a missing pull-up.

q: GPIOA->IDR reads 0x00000024. What is (GPIOA->IDR >> 2) & 1u?
why: 0x24 = 0010 0100: bits 5 and 2 are set. Shifting right by 2 brings bit 2 to bit 0, and & 1 keeps it: 1.

q: Starting from reset (0xEBFFFFFF), what does GPIOA->MODER read after the clear-then-set that makes PA5 an output?
why: Clear bits 11:10: 0xEBFFFFFF & 0xFFFFF3FF = 0xEBFFF3FF. OR in 1 << 10 = 0x400: 0xEBFFF7FF. 0xEBFFF3FF is input (00); 0xEBFFFBFF is AF (10).

q: From reset (0xEBFFFFFF), what does MODER read after making PA6 an output with clear-then-set?
why: PA6 is bits 13:12, mask 0x3000. Clearing gives 0xEBFFCFFF; OR 1 << 12 = 0x1000 gives 0xEBFFDFFF.

q: From reset (0xEBFFFFFF), what does MODER read after setting PA4 to alternate function (10)?
why: PA4 is bits 9:8. Clear: 0xEBFFFCFF. OR 2 << 8 = 0x200: 0xEBFFFEFF. 0xEBFFFDFF would be output (01).

q: Code writes GPIOA->MODER = 1u << 10; to make PA5 an output. What else happens?
choices: Every other pin becomes input, including the debug pins
The write is ignored because MODER is read-only
why: A plain assignment writes the whole register, 0x00000400: 00 (input) for every other pin, PA13/PA14 included. Clear-then-set changes only bits 11:10.

q: Code writes GPIOA->MODER |= 1u << 10; on a pin at its reset value. What mode does PA5 end in?
choices: Input: OR clears the other bit
why: OR can only turn bits on, never off. The field was 11, so it stays 11. The clear step is required.

q: GPIOA->PUPDR reads 0x24000000. What does it read after enabling a pull-up on PA4 with clear-then-set?
why: PA4's field is bits 9:8. Clearing leaves 0x24000000; OR 1 << 8 = 0x100 gives 0x24000100. 0x24000200 would be a pull-down.

q: GPIOA->PUPDR reads 0x24000000. What does it read after a pull-down on PA3?
why: PA3's field is bits 7:6, and pull-down is 10: 2 << 6 = 0x80. 0x24000040 would be a pull-up.

q: From PUPDR = 0x24000000, pull-ups are enabled on PA0 and then PA1. Final value?
why: PA0: 01 in bits 1:0 → 0x1. PA1: 01 in bits 3:2 → 0x4. Together 0x5 = 0101. 0x2400000A would be pull-downs.

q: main() does GPIOA->ODR |= 1u << 5 while an ISR does GPIOA->ODR |= 1u << 6. What can go wrong?
choices: The ISR's change is lost if it lands mid read-modify-write
Nothing: ODR writes are atomic on a single-core Cortex-M0+
Both pins toggle instead of being set
The ISR faults because ODR is in use
why: ODR |= is three instructions. If the ISR runs between main()'s ldr and str, main() writes back a stale copy and PA6 goes off again.

q: Why is GPIOA->BSRR = 1u << 5 safe against an ISR that also changes port A?
choices: It is one store, so it is atomic
BSRR masks interrupts while it is written
BSRR is declared volatile in CMSIS
why: There is nothing to read and nothing stale to write back. An interrupt can land before or after the one store, never inside it.

q: What does writing a 0 to a bit of BSRR do?
why: In BSRR a 0 means 'leave alone'. Only a 1 at bit n (set) or bit n + 16 (reset) changes a pin.

q: Which single line drives PA5 low without touching any other pin?
why: Bit 5 + 16 = 21 is PA5's reset bit. 1u << 5 sets it high, writing 0 does nothing, and ODR has no bit 21 for this.

q: Which single BSRR value sets PB1 high and PB6 low and leaves every other pin of port B alone?
Which BSRR value sets PA3 high and drives PA8 low?
The LED bar uses GPIOB->BSRR = ((uint32_t)(uint8_t)~leds << 16) | leds;. What is written for leds = 0x0F?
why: Low half: 0x0F sets PB0–PB3. ~0x0F as 8 bits is 0xF0, shifted to the reset half: PB4–PB7 off. PB8–PB15 stay untouched.

q: What does GPIOA->BRR = 1u << 5 do?
why: BRR (offset 0x28) is BSRR's reset half on its own: bit n resets pin n. It is write-only and atomic too.

q: MODER = 10 on a pin. What does AFR add?
choices: Whether the pin is push-pull or open-drain
why: MODER = 10 says a peripheral owns the pin; AFR's 4-bit number says which. Neither alone is enough.

q: Where does the AF number for USART2 on PA2 come from?
choices: The datasheet's alternate-function table; it differs per pin
It is always AF1 for every UART
The reference manual's register reset values
It equals the peripheral's IRQ number
why: AF numbers are looked up per pin in the datasheet. USART2 on PA2/PA3 is AF1 here, but another pin or chip may differ.

q: A UART pin has MODER = 10 but the wrong AF number. What does the board do?
choices: Looks configured and carries nothing, with no error
Raises a HardFault on the first write
Falls back to the default peripheral for that pin automatically
Sends data at the wrong baud rate
why: The wrong AF just connects some other peripheral, or nothing. No fault, no error, just a silent pin.

q: PA9 and PA10 are both set to AF1. Assuming AFR[1] started at 0, what does it read?
why: PA9 is AFR[1] bits 7:4 and PA10 bits 11:8, each 0001: 0x00000110. 0x00001100 is AFR[0] with PA2 and PA3 on AF1.

q: In which order does gpio_init() set up a pin?
why: Every peripheral follows clock, configure, use. Without the clock first, every configuration write vanishes.

q: The code configures MODER and writes ODR correctly but never sets RCC->IOPENR for the port. What happens?
choices: Writes vanish and reads return 0, with no error
The LED works, but at a lower speed
A HardFault on the first MODER write
The compiler warns that the RCC clock gate was never set
why: An unclocked port is silently deaf. Both pieces of code look correct, and the LED stays dark.

q: Roughly how does a typical button press bounce?
why: Contacts hit, bounce apart and hit again for about a millisecond. Wokwi models 10 to 100 transitions per press.

q: How does lesson 05's debouncer decide a new level is real?
choices: It is unchanged for DEBOUNCE_MS samples in a row
It appears in the majority of the last 20 samples
It appears at least once in the last 20 ms
It is confirmed by an EXTI edge
why: The level must hold for DEBOUNCE_MS (20) consecutive 1 ms samples. Any change restarts the count.

q: DEBOUNCE_MS = 20, samples every 1 ms. A press bounces, and the last bounce is at t = 3 ms. When is the press reported?
why: Every change restarts the count, so the event comes DEBOUNCE_MS after the last bounce: 3 + 20 = 23 ms.

q: DEBOUNCE_MS = 4, 1 ms samples, 'stable' starts at 0. Raw samples from ms 1: 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 … At which ms is the press reported?
why: The last change is at ms 6. Four more equal samples (ms 7, 8, 9, 10) bring held to 4, so the press is reported at ms 10. ms 9 is counting the change itself as a sample.

q: Polling the button at 1 kHz reports only 1–2 level changes per press. Why?
choices: Sampling is too slow to see most bounces
The button barely bounces at all
The pull-up resistor filters the bounces out
why: Bounces are microseconds apart, samples a millisecond apart, so most bounces fall between samples. Polling is a filter.

q: What weakness of polling does a slow printf in the main loop expose?
choices: The loop doesn't come back in time, so samples are late or missed
printf disables interrupts while it runs
why: Polling depends on the loop coming back. Anything slow delays the next sample, and a pulse shorter than the loop is invisible.

q: printf sends 23 characters at 115 200 baud (10 bits per character). About how long does the loop stall?
why: One character takes 10 / 115 200 ≈ 87 µs, so 23 characters take 230 / 115 200 ≈ 2.0 ms: two missed 1 ms samples. 87 µs is a single character.

q: What is the full interrupt path for a button edge?
why: EXTI turns the edge into a request, the NVIC enables and ranks it, and the vector table gives the handler's address.

q: What are the EXTICR port codes?
why: Codes are 0 = A, 1 = B, 2 = C, 3 = D, 5 = F. Port F is 5, not 4: code 4 would be port E, which this chip doesn't have.

q: A button on PB6 must interrupt. What goes in EXTICR, assuming the register started at 0?
why: Line 6 is in EXTICR[6 / 4] = EXTICR[1], bits 8·(6 mod 4)+7 : 8·2 = 23:16. Port B's code is 1: 1 << 16 = 0x00010000.

q: PF2 is to raise an EXTI interrupt. What goes into EXTICR[0], assuming it started at 0?
why: Line 2 is bits 23:16 of EXTICR[0], and port F's code is 5: 5 << 16 = 0x00050000. 0x00040000 uses the wrong code 4.

q: PA1 and PB1 both need interrupts. What is true?
choices: They share line 1, so only one of them can interrupt
Both work: each GPIO port has its own separate set of 16 EXTI lines
Both work, but at different NVIC priorities
Only PB1 can, because B outranks A
why: Line n watches pin n of one port only: EXTICR is a multiplexer that picks one input.

q: A button on PA1 works even though the code never writes EXTICR. Moved to PC1, it is dead. Why?
choices: Port A's code is 0, the reset value, so PA1 worked by luck
PC1 has no internal pull-up resistor on this 48-pin package
Port C cannot raise interrupts on this chip
EXTICR is only read once, at reset
why: EXTICR resets to 0, which already selects port A. Every other port must be written explicitly.

q: Where is EXTICR on the STM32C0, compared with the STM32F4?
choices: In EXTI on the C0; in SYSCFG on the F4
In SYSCFG on the C0; in EXTI on the F4
why: On the C0, EXTICR is part of EXTI. F4 code using SYSCFG->EXTICR won't compile here.

q: A button with a pull-up is pressed. Which EXTI trigger register catches the press?
why: Active low: pressing takes the pin from 1 to 0, a falling edge. The release is the rising edge.

q: Which line correctly clears line 1's falling-edge pending flag?
why: Pending bits are write 1 to clear, and writing 0 does nothing. |= would also write back other lines' pending 1s and clear them.

q: FPR1 reads 0x00000012. The handler for line 1 runs EXTI->FPR1 |= 1u << 1;. Which pending flags does that clear?
why: |= reads 0x12 and writes back 0x12 | 0x02 = 0x12, a 1 at bits 1 and 4. Write-1-to-clear clears both, so line 4's edge is lost unhandled.

q: During EXTI setup, when should IMR1 be unmasked?
choices: Last, after edges are set and old pending flags are cleared
Before the edge triggers, after the NVIC
It doesn't matter; IMR1 is ignored until reset
why: If you unmask before clearing stale pending flags, an old edge can fire the handler at once.

q: How does the STM32C0 latch edges compared with older STM32 families?
choices: Separately: RPR1 for rising, FPR1 for falling
In one shared PR register for both edges, like older families
Only in the NVIC's ISPR register
why: The C0 has separate rising and falling pending registers. Older families have a single PR.

q: What does writing 0 to a bit of NVIC ISER do?
why: ISER is set-enable: a 1 enables and a 0 is ignored. You disable an IRQ through ICER.

q: NVIC_EnableIRQ for IRQ 7. What does it write to ISER?
why: Bit n = IRQ n: 1 << 7 = 0x80. Writing 0x07 would enable IRQs 0, 1 and 2.

q: NVIC_SetPriority(IRQ 5, 2). What does IPR[1] read, if the other bytes are 0?
why: IRQ 5 is in IPR[5 / 4] = IPR[1], byte 5 mod 4 = 1 (bits 15:8). The value is 2 << 6 = 0x80, shifted 8: 0x00008000.

q: IRQ 7 is set to priority 1, the rest of IPR[1] is 0. What does IPR[1] read?
why: IRQ 7 is byte 3 of IPR[1] (bits 31:24). The value is 1 << 6 = 0x40, so 0x40 << 24 = 0x40000000.

q: EXTI4_15_IRQn is IRQ 7. What is its vector number, and where is the vector?
objdump shows the bytes a5 03 00 08 in a vector slot. Where does the handler's code start?
why: Little-endian: 0x080003A5. Bit 0 is the Thumb bit, so the function itself (nm's address) is 0x080003A4.

q: Which EXTI lines share IRQ 7?
why: IRQ 5 = lines 0–1, IRQ 6 = lines 2–3, IRQ 7 = lines 4–15. IRQ 7 is not 'line 7'.

q: A button on PB9 is set up for an EXTI interrupt. Which IRQ and handler run?
why: PB9 is on line 9, and lines 4–15 share IRQ 7. There is no per-line handler for line 9.

q: Why must EXTI0_1_IRQHandler read the pending bits?
choices: IRQ 5 is shared by lines 0 and 1, so the vector alone doesn't say which fired
To tell the NVIC to stop pending the IRQ
Reading them is what re-enables interrupts
The handler's own priority is stored there
why: Several lines share one vector, and the IRQ can even be pended by software with nothing in EXTI. Never trust the vector; read the pending bit.

q: The handler forgets to clear the EXTI pending bit. What does the board do after the first press?
choices: 'Freezes': the handler runs again and again
Crashes into HardFault on the second interrupt entry
Counts that press, then ignores later ones
why: The NVIC sees the line as long as the bit is set, so the handler re-enters as soon as it returns. It hasn't crashed: it is running flat out.

q: Why doesn't the handler debounce by waiting 20 ms itself?
choices: It would block everything of equal or lower priority for 20 ms
The NVIC aborts handlers after 1 ms
EXTI loses its pending bits after 1 ms
why: Handlers record; main() decides. The handler counts edges, and main() runs a 20 ms 'quiet' stopwatch.

q: b_edges is incremented in the handler and only read by main(), with no lock. Why is that safe?
choices: One aligned 32-bit word, one writer, and volatile
main() always reads it inside a __disable_irq() critical section
why: A single aligned word written by one side can't tear. volatile makes main() reload it each time.

q: With bounce on, button B (interrupt) shows tens of edges per press, but button A (polled) shows 1–2. Which is right?
choices: Both: the interrupt sees every edge; the poll samples a summary
Only A: the interrupt is double-counting
Only B: the polled code has a bug
Neither: Wokwi's bounce model is wrong
why: An interrupt sees every edge, wanted or not; polling filters. They answer different questions.

q: Edges latch in FPR1, but the NVIC never sees the request and the handler never runs. What was forgotten?
choices: Setting the line's bit in IMR1
Clearing the pending bit in the handler
why: IMR1 is the gate between EXTI and the NVIC. Masked, the edge is recorded in FPR1 but goes no further.

q: The NVIC shows IRQ 5 pending, but the handler never runs. What was forgotten?
why: The request reached the NVIC (it is pending) but the IRQ is not enabled in ISER, so it is held.

q: The board hangs on the first press, and nm shows EXTI0_1_IRQHandler as W. What is the cause?
choices: The pending bit is never cleared
The NVIC priority is too high
The IOPENR clock gate is off
why: W means the weak placeholder is still in vector 21, so the press jumps to Default_Handler and loops. Your misspelt function was deleted as dead code.

q: A released button gives random 'phantom' presses. Which of the seven silences is it?
why: Without a pull-up, the released pin floats and reads randomly. A missing input mode reads 0 instead: 'pressed' forever.

q: Which interrupt bug is the opposite of the seven 'silences'?
choices: Not clearing the pending bit: the handler runs forever
A misspelt handler name that the linker silently replaces
why: The seven give silence. Forgetting to clear the pending bit gives too much: the handler re-enters forever.

q: Which switch in the interrupt path starts out on?
why: Every other switch on the path resets off. PRIMASK resets to 0, so interrupts are globally on.

q: In the debugger, which register write fakes an edge on EXTI line 1 with no button?
why: SWIER1 is EXTI's software trigger: writing 1 at bit n is an edge on line n, and it sets the pending bit. IDR is read-only.

q: IRQ 5 is pended with NVIC->ISPR = 32 and no EXTI edge. What does the handler do?
choices: Enters, finds no pending bit, and counts nothing
Counts one edge, exactly as if the button had been pressed
Hangs, because nothing clears the pending bit
why: The NVIC runs the handler, but RPR1/FPR1 are empty so its if is false. That is correct: never trust the vector, read the pending bit.

q: Where should you put a breakpoint to stop once per real press?
choices: Where the event is decided, e.g. d->stable = raw;
On the first line of debounce_step(), which runs every millisecond
why: b_edges++ stops on every bounce edge, and debounce_step() runs 1000 times a second. Break where the event is decided.
